title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
Pixels with Purpose


How to Amplify the Impact of Your Talk Through Visual Reinforcement

title: Pixels with Purpose
text: The goal of any talk is audience impact.

title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
Slides don’t drive impact.


The talk drives impact.


Slides simply reinforce the talk.



Slides are not where a talk starts.
Don’t worry! We WILL talk about slides. We just want to be clear that slides are not where a talk starts.

title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
So what does reinforcement actually mean?



Image source: https://unsplash.com/photos/man-standing-beside-rock-formation-mj51pZwan9c

title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
Hold their attention.


Help them understand what’s being presented.


Enable them to retain what matters most.




Keep the audience’s attention — the talk is bound by time and attention
Understand and care about the information — by directly reinforcing what the speaker is saying
Remember it — dual-encoding with multiple senses (hearing and seeing); brain science backs up that using multiple senses aids retention

What slides should not (primarily) do: remind the speaker what they’re supposed to be (although they can be a visual aid to keep the speaker on track; that’s just a natural artifact if they do their primary job well!)
Image source: https://unsplash.com/photos/man-standing-beside-rock-formation-mj51pZwan9c

title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
Iconic Memory


Pre-Cognition





Short-Term Memory


7 ± 2





Long-Term Memory


In an Hour,Tomorrow,Next Month


The human brain has limitations:

Iconic memory — pre-cognition; everything comes in and gets processed
Short-term memory / Miller’s Law (7 +/- 2) - George Miller, psychologist in the 1950s
Long-term memory

title: Pixels with Purpose
text: Minimize cognitive load.

title: Pixels with Purpose
section: How many 5s are in this set of numbers?
text:
How many 5s are in this set of numbers?


4979027564790289472862409240603707057027 0802900730250127023700837408207872027200 0260270379377570970737797066746209709470 7970972309723097959275092727979873497260



Source: Information Dashboard Design by Stephen Few


Opportunity to experience cognitive load: counting the 5s without them highlighted. Then count them with them highlighted. So much easier, even though only a tiny number of pixels on the screen were altered.

title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
Maximize the data-pixel ratio!

This concept was initially put forth by Edward Tufte as “the data-ink ratio,” and Stephen Few later modernized it as “the data-pixel ratio.”




Data-Information Pixels


All Non-Background Pixels



  Every pixel that is notsimply the background color
 Pixels that representactual data or information

(After build) This is an example of a slide with high cognitive load.
Call out: let’s see what happens if we remove all of those non-data-information pixels!
Image source: https://unsplash.com/photos/candlestick-stock-chart-on-dark-screen-VLpWpv3oDB4

title: Pixels with Purpose
text:
Data-Information Pixels


All Non-Background Pixels



 Every pixel that is notsimply the background color
 Pixels that representactual data or information

We’ve drastically increased the data-pixel ratio, which gives the brain fewer choices to make as to what to try to take in and process.
When I removed all the extra clutter, I actually had more room on the slide, which then let me make the ratio itself larger on the screen.

The application of the revised preprocessing technique that the team developed during the second quarter resulted in a measurable reduction in the overall run-time of the production model, with observed improvements generally falling in the range of approximately 30 to 40 percent.

While this may be an accurate statement, it’s a LOT to read. We’ve all seen slides like this.

The first thing we can do is simply trim the words! Be more economical.

title: Pixels with Purpose
section: Predicting the body mass of penguins
text:
Predicting the body mass of penguins

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000,
         species = as.factor(species),
         island = as.factor(island),
         sex = as.factor(sex))

model_spec <- lm(body_mass_kg ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm +
                   bill_depth_mm + species + sex,
                 data = penguins_clean)

model_summary <- broom::tidy(model_spec, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)

model_summary |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))


This is the default. It may seem fine on your screen now, but it WILL BE TOO MUCH and it WILL BE TOO SMALL when presented

Also, don’t expect all cultural references to land with the entire audience: Star Trek, pop culture, memes.
And, obviously, steer clear of anything potentially offensive.

Zero references found anywhere

Size

371 KB

None of these five turned up in comments, .notes blocks, R chunks, or anywhere else — they are simply absent from the codebase, not conditionally referenced. Safe to delete, but confirm before deleting closeupeye-bw-og.jpg and pic_uncle_sam.png specifically, since they look like intentionally-kept “before” versions of images still in use.
Flagged for manual confirmation (not literal filename matches)
None found. Every image reference in the project is a literal images/filename.ext string — in Pandoc ![]() syntax, background-image= attributes, or the logo: YAML field. There are no computed/variable paths (e.g., no R string-interpolated image paths, no Sass url() calls) and no filenames appearing only inside comments. This makes the “zero references” list above reliable as-is, with no gray-area cases to separate out.
All other images — reference counts
Every remaining file in images/ has at least one confirmed literal reference; several (meadowlark-logo.png, down-arrow.png, left-up-arc-arrow.png, left-down-arc-arrow.png, pic_cognitive_load.jpg, norm_conform_frustrated.png) are intentionally reused 2–3 times across slides/decks. Full per-file reference tables are omitted here for brevity but were verified line-by-line during this audit.
Side note (not an asset, but adjacent)
images/.DS_Store is a macOS Finder artifact, not a real asset. It’s harmless but doesn’t belong in the repo. Worth adding .DS_Store to .gitignore if it isn’t already covered — a quick check shows the root .gitignore exists but you may want to confirm it covers this path.
Human Feedback

Remove all zero-reference images found. This includes closeupeye-bw-og.jpg and pic_uncle_sam.png, which both have, indeed, been superseded.

Notify me if there are any other changes recommended in this section that I have not addressed with this feedback.

2. SCSS Naming Consistency
Overall finding: the file is unusually consistent. All custom classes use kebab-case with no camelCase and effectively no snake_case (checked explicitly — zero camelCase identifiers found in class or variable names). The one real inconsistency is isolated to a single concept name:
Proposed rename: muted_med → muted-med
The Sass variable $muted_med and the CSS custom property --brand-muted_med are the only identifiers in the file using an underscore. Every sibling variable ($primary, $secondary, $accent, $muted, $body-color, $body-bg, $link-color, $divider-text, $body-light, $footer-baseline, all the $presentation-* tokens) is kebab-case or a single word.

Blast radius outside styles.scss: none. I checked whether var(--brand-muted_med) is consumed anywhere in the .qmd files — it isn’t (see next paragraph). So this rename is fully contained to styles.scss.
Do NOT rename brand$muted_med in dataviz-best-practices.qmd:51, _05-example-table.qmd:155,249,251 — that’s an R list name following R’s own snake_case convention, deliberately independent from the Sass variable (the comment at styles.scss:41 explicitly notes hex values are hardcoded in R separately). Renaming the Sass side doesn’t touch these at all.
Related finding (context, not a rename): most --brand-* custom properties are unused
While tracing blast radius for the rename above, I found that only --divider-bg (of the seven properties exposed in the :root block, styles.scss:42–51) is actually consumed via var() anywhere in the .qmd files (9 uses, all background-color="var(--divider-bg)"). --brand-bg, --brand-primary, --brand-secondary, --brand-accent, --brand-dark, --brand-muted, and --brand-muted_med are all defined but currently dead — not a naming issue, just relevant context for why the --brand-muted_med rename above carries zero external risk. Not proposing removal since that’s outside this audit’s scope (naming, not usage-pruning) — flagging only so it isn’t mistaken for a wider blast radius than it has.
Naming collision worth flagging (not a rename)
.callout-tip (styles.scss:463) reuses the exact name Quarto uses for its own built-in callout block type (::: {.callout-tip}). It’s currently unused in any .qmd file, so there’s no active conflict, but the name is a trap: if anyone ever adds a native Quarto callout to either deck, it will silently pick up this custom styling instead of (or blended with) Quarto’s built-in callout CSS. Since it’s unused, this is a candidate for either renaming to something project-specific (e.g. .highlight-box) or deleting outright — your call, flagging rather than proposing since deletion/rename both need your sign-off given it’s a name collision rather than a pure style inconsistency.
Everything else checked and found consistent

No BEM-style patterns (__/-- modifiers) exist anywhere, so there’s nothing to make consistent on that front.
Multi-part utility families are internally consistent: text-panel-{side}-{width}, memory-detail-{n}-{n}, callout-{oval,rect,line-vertical,label}, slide-body-{med,lg}-text[-emphasis], norm-{conform,speech,advice}, rotate-{ccw,cw}-15, kable-table[-borders|-light].
Two classes produce visually identical output — .title-text and .slide-body-heading p share one rule block (styles.scss:87–95) by design (comma-joined selector), not an accidental duplication — flagging only as an FYI, not a defect.

Human Feedback

Rename muted_med → muted-med in the SCSS as proposed
Confirmed: do not rename brand$muted_med in the .qmd files
I’ve added a Deferred section to the bottom of this document that we will come back to after completing the initial audit areas to address further cleanup of the palette configuration approach.
Go ahead and remove .callout-tip from the .scss to prevent future confusion.

title: Data Viz Presentations
Data Viz Presentations
text:
4. QMD Syntax/Layout Consistency
All of the following are cosmetic — none change parsed structure, heading levels, or fenced-div nesting depth. Verified render-safety by checking Pandoc’s fenced-div and attribute-parsing rules before including anything here.
Safe to batch

Fenced-div class syntax: bare word vs. braced dot-class. normative-conformity.qmd uses bare ::: columns / :::: columns (lines 63, 89, 110) where every other file uses ::: {.columns} / :::: {.columns} (6 instances across _05-example-table.qmd and dataviz-best-practices.qmd:81). Pandoc treats ::: className and ::: {.className} identically — purely a style choice. Recommend standardizing on the braced form since it’s already the 2:1 majority convention.
Space between fence marker and opening brace. 14 instances of :::{ (no space) vs. 303 instances of ::: { / :::: { (with space):

_04-example-line-chart.qmd:3,79,124,217
_06-example-text.qmd:13,22,34 Pandoc doesn’t require the space; recommend adding it to match the dominant style.

fragment-index attribute quoting. Quoted (fragment-index="1") in _04-example-line-chart.qmd (8 instances) vs. unquoted (fragment-index=1) in _02-cognitive-load.qmd (16 instances) and _03-data-pixel-ratio.qmd (6 instances). Both parse identically as a Quarto/reveal attribute; recommend picking one (unquoted is the majority, 22 vs 8).
Double space after heading marker. _01-intro.qmd:15 — ##  {.center ...} (two spaces) vs. every other bare-attribute heading in the project using a single space. One-line fix.
Class/attribute ordering within fenced-div and span attribute lists. .fragment appears in every possible position — first (_01-intro.qmd:22 {.fragment .slide-body-heading}), last (_01-intro.qmd:54 {.slide-body-heading .fragment}, normative-conformity.qmd:64 {.column width="50%" .center-col .norm-speech .fragment}), and middle (_02-cognitive-load.qmd:14 {.absolute .memory-detail .memory-detail-1-5 .fragment .fade-in-then-out ...}). This is scattered across roughly 30 attribute blocks in _01-intro.qmd, _02-cognitive-load.qmd, _03-data-pixel-ratio.qmd, _04-example-line-chart.qmd, and normative-conformity.qmd. Attribute order inside {...} has no effect on Pandoc/reveal.js rendering, so this is safe to normalize — recommend a fixed convention, e.g., positioning/structural classes → .fragment/animation classes → fragment-index → geometry attrs (top/left/width) → style last, and I’d want you to confirm the convention before I touch ~30 lines rather than guessing at your preference.

Uncertain — needs discussion (not proposed as safe fixes)

Nested fenced-div colon counts. index.qmd:81–94 opens with :::: {.columns} (4 colons) but a directly-nested ::: {.column width="62%"} (3 colons) itself contains two more 3-colon divs (.title-text, .subtitle-text) at the same colon count as their parent. Pandoc’s fence-matching algorithm can be sensitive to this (“outer fence needs ≥ colons of anything it contains” is the safe convention; matching counts on parent/child is technically allowed but is exactly the kind of thing that renders correctly today and breaks on a Pandoc version bump or minor edit). This currently renders fine, but I’m not proposing to “fix” the colon counts since a wrong edit here is a real rendering-breakage risk — this needs your explicit review, not a batch pass.
<br> vs. other line-break mechanisms. Raw HTML <br> is used ~13 times across 5 files for forced line breaks in short text. Separately, _02-cognitive-load.qmd:64–67 uses a trailing backslash (\) at end-of-line inside .digit-wall to force line breaks within one dense block of digits. These aren’t really serving the same purpose (short thematic breaks vs. exact wrapping inside a single content block), so “unifying” them isn’t obviously correct — surfacing this so you can decide if it’s worth touching, not proposing a change.

Human Feedback

Standardize on the braced form for the class syntax throughout
Add a space between the fence marker and the opening brace throughout (go with what’s already dominant)
Go with unquoted fragment-index throughout
Change the double space after the heading marker in the one instance found to be a single space
For the class/attribute ordering, update all to use: positioning/structural classes → .fragment/animation classes → fragment-index → geometry attrs (top/left/width) → style last
Update to follow the “outer fence needs ≥ colons of anything it contains” convention throughout all of the .qmd files. Search every .qmd file in the project for nested fenced-div blocks (:::/::::) where an outer fence’s colon count is NOT strictly greater than any fence nested inside it. For each occurrence, increase the outer fence’s colon count so it’s strictly greater than the highest colon count of anything nested inside it, following the “outer fence needs more colons than anything it contains” convention. Only ever increase colon counts — never decrease any fence’s colon count, even if it looks like it would still work with fewer.
Go ahead and replace the trailing backslash (‘\’) with <br> on the one slide where it occurs.

title: Data Viz Presentations
text:
Summary — Risk Tiers
Lowest-risk, safe to batch together

SCSS: $muted_med → $muted-med and --brand-muted_med → --brand-muted-med rename (7 lines, all in styles.scss, zero external consumers).
QMD: fenced-div bare-class → braced-class in normative-conformity.qmd (3 lines).
QMD: no-space :::{ → ::: { (7 lines across 2 files).
QMD: fragment-index quoting standardization (24 lines across 2 files) — pick unquoted (majority) or quoted, either is safe.
QMD: double-space fix in _01-intro.qmd:15 (1 line).
Housekeeping: delete the 5 zero-reference images, and add .DS_Store to .gitignore if not already covered.

Needs your explicit decision before touching

.fragment/class ordering standardization (~30 attribute blocks) — safe mechanically, but needs you to pick the target convention first.
.callout-tip naming collision with Quarto’s built-in callout type — rename vs. delete (it’s currently unused either way).
SCSS section reorganization (item 3) — mechanically safe (pure reordering + comment headers) except for the three specificity-tied groups (A, B, C above), which must stay in their current relative order unless you decide to also resolve the underlying overlap (e.g., by adding a distinguishing modifier or scoping one of them more tightly).
closeupeye-bw-og.jpg and pic_uncle_sam.png deletion — high confidence these are superseded originals, but worth a quick visual diff against their replacements before deleting since they’re meaningfully large files.

Out of scope / do not touch

Nested fenced-div colon-count pattern in index.qmd — real rendering risk, not cosmetic.
<br> vs. backslash hard-break — different use cases, not a clear inconsistency.
Any reveal.js/Quarto built-in class or selector (.reveal, .slides, section, .fragment itself, .slide-logo, .footer, .columns/.column as Quarto’s own layout primitive, heading levels).
